title: NASA Opens First New Wind Tunnel in Over 40 Years at Langley
excerpt: The $57 million Flight Dynamics Research Facility replaces two aging tunnels and will support Artemis lunar missions, Mars research, and next-generation aircraft testing.
body:
• NASA's $57 million Flight Dynamics Research Facility opened July 31 at Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia — the agency's first new wind tunnel in more than four decades.
  • The facility replaces two tunnels dating to 1939 and 1941, and will support the Artemis lunar program, Mars mission research, and autonomous aircraft testing.
  • Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, an Indian American born in Hyderabad, joined NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman at the ribbon-cutting ceremony.

NASA cut the ribbon on a state-of-the-art wind tunnel at its Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, on July 31 — the agency's first major new wind tunnel facility in more than four decades. The 25,000-square-foot Flight Dynamics Research Facility, built at a cost of $57 million, is designed to test everything from autonomous drones and experimental aircraft to spacecraft returning from the Moon.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine, Rep. Bobby Scott, and General Services Administration Administrator Edward Forst attended the ceremony, according to the Washington Examiner.

"The Flight Dynamics Research Facility, the first NASA wind tunnel in over 40 years, makes a revolutionary step forward in how we test everything from aircraft to spacecraft."

— Trina Dyal, Director, NASA Langley Research Center

What the Facility Does

The FDRF is a large subsonic vertical wind tunnel with a test section measuring 20 feet in diameter and 24 feet high. It can generate airspeeds from 0 to 117 mph, allowing researchers to study how aircraft and spacecraft behave in flight — including their stability, controllability, free-fall characteristics, spins, and spin recovery.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=wntmttHQIW0

Researchers drop scale models into a rising vertical airflow, simulating real flight conditions. During the ceremony, Isaacman demonstrated the tunnel by launching a scaled-down model of the Artemis program's Orion spacecraft into the airflow.

Replacing a Legacy

The new tunnel replaces two of Langley's longest-serving facilities: the 12-Foot Low-Speed Tunnel, which began operations in 1939, and the 20-Foot Vertical Spin Tunnel, opened in 1941. Between them, the two tunnels supported research on nearly every U.S. military aircraft designed since World War II, along with major NASA programs including the X-29, X-31, and the X-59 quiet supersonic research aircraft.

By consolidating their capabilities into a single modern facility, NASA says it will deliver greater performance while cutting maintenance and operating costs. Much of the older tunnels' equipment — test rigs, instrumentation, data systems — has been repurposed for the FDRF, according to NASA.

"You don't want to have so much of your budget maintaining the past that comes with the expense of the mission of today and tomorrow. This is a perfect example of doing the right thing."

— Jared Isaacman, NASA Administrator

Supporting Artemis and Beyond

The facility's most consequential role will be supporting NASA's return to the Moon and longer-term Mars ambitions. Researchers will use the FDRF to test entry, descent, and landing technologies — the most dangerous phases of any space mission. The tunnel will help evaluate how vehicles behave as they descend through an atmosphere, reducing risk before actual flights.

Beyond space exploration, the FDRF will support a rapidly evolving aviation landscape. Researchers plan to use it for testing advanced aircraft concepts, autonomous flight vehicles, drones, and emerging technologies like air taxis — an area drawing significant investment from companies worldwide, including several Indian-founded startups in the urban air mobility sector.

Indian American Presence at the Ceremony

Among the dignitaries at the ribbon-cutting was Virginia Lt. Gov. Ghazala Hashmi, who was born in Hyderabad, India, and is the first Indian American and first Muslim woman elected to statewide office in Virginia. Her presence underscores the growing representation of Indian Americans in public life across technology and aerospace hubs like Virginia's Hampton Roads region, home to Langley and a cluster of defense and space contractors that employ a substantial Indian-origin workforce.

What's Next

The FDRF is expected to begin supporting active research programs soon. Its opening comes against the backdrop of recent tensions over NASA's budget — the Trump administration proposed closing five unspecified wind tunnels and cutting Langley's workforce in 2025, though Congress largely restored funding in January 2026.

Sen. Warner acknowledged the turbulence. "It's been rough the last year-plus for federal employees, and we lost too many folks at NASA," he said. "The fact that we are now rebuilding that, bringing more people in, is an enormous benefit."

The 25-year effort behind the FDRF, driven by retired chief engineer Mike Fremaux, signals NASA's commitment to modernizing its ground-testing infrastructure even as the agency juggles tight budgets and an expanding mission portfolio.
